fixes.explanation: That's the one, baker. Paul says some in Corinth were saying there is no resurrection of the dead, even though it's preached that Christ has been raised (1 Corinthians 15:12). He asks how both can be true. It's like handing someone a warm cookie and telling them cookies don't exist.

Paul doesn't say their faith would be hidden. He says it would be futile (1 Corinthians 15:17). Hidden is how I spent years, stuck in the back of a junk drawer, friend. Futile is the word on the page.

That's his line. “If our hope in Christ is for this life alone, we are to be pitied more than all men.” (1 Corinthians 15:19). Notice the condition: it's only if their hope in Christ stops at this life. Paul is showing how much rides on the resurrection.
Paul never says fear here. He says they would be pitied more than all men (1 Corinthians 15:19). Pity is the word he uses for believers whose hope in Christ is for this life alone.
Yes, Adam, the first man (1 Corinthians 15:45). Paul says, “For as in Adam all die…” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Death came through him, and Paul is about to show who brings life.
Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is a great name, but Paul doesn't use him here. He puts Adam and Christ side by side (1 Corinthians 15:22). Those are the two men in the sentence.
Abraham, Israel's forefather (Genesis 12:2), doesn't show up in this verse. Paul names Adam, through whom all die, and Christ, in whom all will be made alive (1 Corinthians 15:22). Just those two.

That's the one. “The last enemy to be destroyed is death.” (1 Corinthians 15:26). Death goes last, and it goes down. Paul says just before this that Christ must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet (1 Corinthians 15:25).

Paul doesn't name Satan in this verse. He says the last enemy to be destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:26). Right before that, he says Christ must reign until He has put all His enemies under His feet (1 Corinthians 15:25), and death is named as the last of them.

That's what he says. “And when all things have been subjected to Him, then the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all.” (1 Corinthians 15:28). Verse 27 helps here: when it says everything has been put under the Son, this clearly does not include the One who put everything under Him (1 Corinthians 15:27). In other words, the Son is made subject to the Father, and the reason Paul gives is so that God may be all in all.

Paul actually says it, friend. When all things have been subjected to the Son, the Son Himself will be made subject to Him who put all things under Him, so that God may be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28). That's why this one is true. The One who put everything under the Son isn't included in what's put under Him (1 Corinthians 15:27).
That's it, friend. Paul says, “I face death every day, brothers…” (1 Corinthians 15:31). Every day, not once in a while. I think that's a heavy thing to carry.
Not quite, friend. Paul says he faces death every day, not every year (1 Corinthians 15:31). He's talking daily, and I think that's heavy to hear.

That's the saying Paul quotes: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” (1 Corinthians 15:32). He brings it up as what would be said if the dead are not raised. That's the condition, friend, and the if is what matters.

Paul says the opposite, friend. He warns them not to be deceived, and the saying he gives is “Bad company corrupts good character.” (1 Corinthians 15:33). The company they keep does matter, according to him. Keep an eye on who's in your kitchen.
Right. Paul warns them not to be deceived, then says, “Bad company corrupts good character.” (1 Corinthians 15:33). So company does have an effect on character. That's the warning in his words.
